---
title: "Methodology"
subtitle: "A transparent, evidence-based definition of approximately normal"
---

## The simulation unit

For a candidate sample size `n`, one repetition generates `n` observations and computes one sample mean. Repeating this `B = 10,000` times produces the simulated sampling distribution of the sample mean.

The project uses a coarse-to-fine search. The initial grid is deliberately broad; earlier exploratory centers are retained for reproducibility. Targeted population-specific grids in `R/config.R` investigate smaller candidates and nearby larger values. The explicit judgment inputs are in `results/decisions.csv`; these are evidence decisions, not simulation outputs or automatic p-value cutoffs.

## Evidence used together

Each candidate sample size is assessed with a histogram, a theoretical normal overlay when appropriate, a normal Q-Q plot, skewness, excess kurtosis, empirical mean, empirical SE, theoretical mean and SE where valid, and `qq_rmse`.

The Standard Normal population is simulated repeatedly as a calibration benchmark. Its diagnostic ranges show how much skewness, kurtosis, and Q-Q RMSE can fluctuate at `B = 10,000` even when the sampling distribution is exactly normal. This benchmark contextualizes, rather than mechanically decides, the other cases.

## Assumptions and exceptions

The ordinary iid finite-variance CLT does not apply unchanged to every case. Cauchy has no population mean or variance. The dependent failure process requires covariance terms in the variance of a mean. The basketball process is independent but non-identically distributed and uses the variance formula `sum(p_i * (1 - p_i)) / n^2`, not an iid shortcut.

The age-at-death population is synthetic and uses the instructor-provided discrete mixture exactly; it is not historical mortality data.

## Decision rule

The goal is the smallest tested `n` I can defend, not the largest or nicest-looking plot. I assess the histogram, systematic Q-Q curvature, skewness, kurtosis, mean and SE agreement where valid, and nearby larger values together. Small discrete steps or residual tail bends may be acceptable for a practical approximation, but not for precise extreme-tail calculations. The Normal benchmark shows simulation noise; matching that noise is not a requirement.

There is no sharp biological or mathematical transition in these finite-variance cases. Adjacent candidates can be essentially indistinguishable. Where I cannot convincingly reject a smaller candidate, I report a borderline range rather than manufacture a failure reason. A selected value is a judgment under a stated tolerance, not proof that every smaller integer fails.

## Sensitivity to the random seed

The primary run uses the confirmed student seed `7616`. The pipeline repeats the same simulation design with seed `7617` and stores those rows in `results/sensitivity_diagnostics.csv`. Exact skewness, kurtosis, and Q-Q RMSE values move because they are Monte Carlo estimates, but the broad conclusions are not seed-shopped: the exact Normal case remains exact in theory, Cauchy remains highly unstable through `n = 5,000`, and the slower finite-variance cases remain slower than the die and age mixture.

The final selections are recorded in `results/final_summary.csv` by `scripts/finalize_summary.R`. That script checks that every finite selected value is an actual tested row before copying its generated diagnostics into the summary.
